items.title: filelock: SoftFileLock evicts a fresh lock file whose watched age another local user's pre-dated file passed on through inode reuse
items.description:
`SoftFileLock` and `MarkerSoftFileLock` evict an unparsable marker (the lock file at `<path>`, whose presence says a process holds the lock) once a waiting contender has watched it unchanged for two seconds. `SoftFileLease` expires a lease the same way. The watch tells two looks apart by the marker's modification time (mtime) and inode number (the kernel's identity for a file, independent of its name) alone.

Another local user (the other user below) who can create files in the lock's directory, a sticky `/tmp` included (the sticky bit is a directory flag that lets only a file's owner remove it), parks an empty file of its own at the lock path. It dates that file to a future tick of the kernel's coarse clock (a clock that advances in steps of 4 ms), lets the waiters of the user running the lock (the lock user below) watch it past two seconds, and unlinks it in that tick. On a filesystem that hands a freed inode number straight back (ext4, overlayfs on ext4) the lock user's next marker repeats both values. It inherits the time spent watching the other user's file, and a second waiter removes it while its owner holds the lock.

Two of the lock user's processes then run the critical section together with no error. A `SoftFileLease` waiter takes a live lease that its owner wrote moments before, within milliseconds instead of after `lease_duration`. Affected versions: filelock >= 4.1.0 and <= 4.2.0 (finding `ANT-2026-RKC48J5B`).

## Severity

**CVSS:3.1/AV:L/AC:H/PR:L/UI:N/S:U/C:N/I:H/A:N, 4.7 (Medium).**

`AV:L` (local): the other user needs an account on the same host. `AC:H` (high attack complexity): a race the other user cannot steer. It needs ext4-style inode reuse, a coarse-clock timestamp tick the other user can predict, and two polls of the lock user inside a 4 ms tick and a ~75 µs create-to-write gap. The scanner measured 2 to 10 % of attempts; none of our own 250 attempts fired. `PR:L` (low privileges): an unprivileged account is enough. `UI:N` (no user interaction): the lock user's processes act on their own. `C:N` (no confidentiality impact): the other user reads nothing. `I:H` (high integrity impact): two holders write the data the lock protects, and neither learns of the other. `A:N` (no availability impact): the lock keeps working.

Classification from the review: security, conditional, by mechanism. It is the same cross-UID primitive (a UID is a user account's numeric id) as the stale-break inode-reuse race reported in a separate advisory: an inode number reused after the other user's unlink in a sticky directory, which our review reproduced across UIDs, plus a forged future mtime. The scanner rated it high (CWE-694) and demonstrated it across UIDs in its own runs. It did not fire in 250 attempts of ours over ext4 with inode reuse confirmed, nor in the scanner-side triage, so its cross-user claim rests on the report's own runs and on the mechanism.

## Scope and preconditions

- The other user can create files in the lock's directory; a root-owned `1777` directory is enough. It creates, `utime`s (sets the timestamps of) and unlinks only its own file. In the sticky directory its `unlink`, `rename`, `open(..., "w")` and `utime` on a marker of the lock user all fail, and deleting its own file only frees the lock.
- The directory is on a filesystem that reuses a freed inode number at once: ext4, and overlayfs on it (thousands of create/unlink cycles returned one number). tmpfs does not reuse one, so the pair cannot repeat there; btrfs does not either.
- File timestamps come from a coarse clock whose future values the other user can compute (`CLOCK_REALTIME_COARSE`, 4 ms steps on Linux 6.1; 20,000 file creations all carried that clock's value).
- At least two processes of the lock user are waiting on the lock while the other user's file is there. The other user does not choose which processes overlap or when; each attempt blocks the lock for 2.2 s (for a lease, `lease_duration`).
- No symbolic link, hard link or FIFO takes part, so the `fs.protected_*` sysctls (Linux settings that restrict following links and opening pipes in sticky world-writable directories) play no part. `StrictSoftFileLock` keys its watch the same way but only raises `SoftFileLockProtocolError`, so it breaks no lock there.

filelock's checks against another local user hold only when no other user can replace the lock's directory or any of its ancestors. That is the case when each ancestor belongs to the lock user or root and is either not writable by others or sticky. A user who can rename entries in a non-sticky directory above the lock controls every name below it. No file-based lock can defend against that.

## Affected code

At the scanned commit b831496, the watch is [`SoftFileLock._marker_unchanged_for`](https://github.com/tox-dev/filelock/blob/b831496b0273ecd11bf02b8d080ca8b673a538c1/src/filelock/_soft.py#L125-L132), with its caller in [`_try_break_stale_lock`](https://github.com/tox-dev/filelock/blob/b831496b0273ecd11bf02b8d080ca8b673a538c1/src/filelock/_soft.py#L107-L123). The [`MarkerSoftFileLock`](https://github.com/tox-dev/filelock/blob/b831496b0273ecd11bf02b8d080ca8b673a538c1/src/filelock/_marker.py#L74-L81) and [`SoftFileLease`](https://github.com/tox-dev/filelock/blob/b831496b0273ecd11bf02b8d080ca8b673a538c1/src/filelock/_lease.py#L229-L256) paths hand an unparsable marker to the same code. The re-check in [`break_lock_file`](https://github.com/tox-dev/filelock/blob/b831496b0273ecd11bf02b8d080ca8b673a538c1/src/filelock/_util.py#L113-L118) compares the values the contender just read.

## Introduced

0f7c4d3794dc ("fix(soft): expire leases on the contender's clock", #796, 2026-10-07), first released in 4.1.0 (verified against the tags). Earlier releases compared the marker's mtime with the wall clock, and this does not affect them.

## Mechanism

`SoftFileLock._acquire` creates the marker with `O_CREAT | O_EXCL` (create the file, fail if it exists) and only then writes the holder record. In between it calls `fstat` and `uname`, stats `/proc/self/ns/pid` and reads `/proc/<pid>/stat`, so for about 75 µs (measured) the marker exists and is empty. A contender that polls in that gap must not take the marker for garbage, and the check that protects it is the two-second watch. `_try_break_stale_lock` reads the marker, finds no holder, and calls `break_lock_file(lock_file, mtime, ino)` only if `_marker_unchanged_for(mtime, ino)` reaches `MALFORMED_LOCK_AGE_THRESHOLD` (2.0 s). That function keeps `self._marker_seen = ((mtime, ino), first seen)` across polls and returns the elapsed monotonic time (time from a clock that only moves forward) while the pair repeats.

Neither half of the pair belongs to one file. A file's owner sets its mtime to any value with `utime`, a future time included, and ext4 gives the inode number of an unlinked file to the next file created in the directory.

1. While the lock is free, the other user creates an empty file at the lock path (inode `I`) and sets its mtime to `T`, a tick of the coarse clock about 2.2 s in the future.
2. Every waiting process of the lock user polls each 50 ms, reads an empty file and records `_marker_seen = ((T, I), first seen)`. After 2 s each poll calls `break_lock_file`, whose `rename` fails with `EPERM` (operation not permitted; seen with `strace`): the directory is sticky and the file belongs to the other user. `suppress(OSError, ...)` swallows the error, the file stays, and nothing resets `_marker_seen`.
3. When the coarse clock reaches `T`, the other user unlinks its file. Inode `I` is free.
4. Process F of the lock user polls during tick `T`. Its `O_EXCL` create succeeds, and its marker is inode `I` with mtime `T`.
5. Process S polls before F has written its record. It reads an empty file with pair `(T, I)`, `_marker_unchanged_for` returns the 2.2 s that S spent watching the other user's file, and S calls `break_lock_file(lock_file, T, I)`.
6. `break_lock_file` compares mtime and inode before and after its rename, but with the values S just read from F's marker, so both checks pass. F's marker has S's UID, so the rename and the unlink succeed.
7. F writes its record into the unlinked inode and returns from `acquire()`. The path is empty, so the next contender to poll creates a marker and returns from `acquire()` too. F's release finds another inode at the path (`_unlink_open_marker`) and leaves it. Neither holder learns anything.

Step 4 needs a poll inside one 4 ms tick, and step 5 a second poll inside F's 75 µs gap. Step 5 is far likelier than independent 50 ms timers would make it, because contenders that wait together bunch. With filelock's DEBUG messages timestamped, nine waiters polled within 2 to 3 ms of one another, several 0.1 ms apart or closer. In a run where the other user also recorded what replaced its file, 13 of 100 successors appeared in tick `T`, and a waiter broke 7 of those 13.

`MarkerSoftFileLock` and `SoftFileLease` hand an unparsable marker to the same code, and the lease uses the clock a second time, for expiry: `if owner.mode == "lease" and self._marker_unchanged_for(mtime, ino) >= self._lease_duration: break_lock_file(...)`. `_marker_seen` is one attribute, so the same empty file primes this branch, and step 5 has no gap to hit. To every waiter, F's complete lease record with pair `(T, I)` has gone unrefreshed for `lease_duration`, until F's first heartbeat (the periodic refresh a lease holder runs). With the lock user's processes using `SoftFileLease(path, lease_duration=2)` and holding for 1 s, the same other user produced an overlap in 17 of 30 attempts. The superseded holder's `on_compromise` (the callback that tells a holder it lost the lock) reported `owner-changed` 0.67 s after it had entered, at its first heartbeat; a holder that releases before that is not told at all.

## Reproduction

The scanner's reproducer for finding `ANT-2026-RKC48J5B`, as received, ran against commit b831496b0273ecd11bf02b8d080ca8b673a538c1. The `repro` script drives the files under `repro.d/`.

**`repro`**

```python
#!/usr/bin/env python3
import os
import shutil
import subprocess
import sys
import time

LOCK_DIR = "/tmp/locks"
LOCK_PATH = "/tmp/locks/app.lock"
HOLDS_LOG = "/tmp/holds.log"


def start_victims():
    # a root-owned sticky directory like /tmp, and ten processes of user victim taking turns on one lock in it
    shutil.rmtree(LOCK_DIR, ignore_errors=True)
    os.mkdir(LOCK_DIR)
    os.chmod(LOCK_DIR, 0o1777)
    victim = [sys.executable, "/tmp/repro.d/victim.py", LOCK_PATH]
    with open(HOLDS_LOG, "w") as holds_log:
        return [
            subprocess.Popen(victim, stdout=holds_log, user="victim", group="victim", extra_groups=[])
            for _ in range(10)
        ]


def holds_entered_after(moment):
    holds = []
    for line in open(HOLDS_LOG):
        fields = dict(field.split("=") for field in line.split())
        hold = {"entered": float(fields["entered"]), "exited": float(fields["exited"]), "line": line.strip()}
        if hold["entered"] > moment:
            holds.append(hold)
    return sorted(holds, key=lambda hold: hold["entered"])


def attack_until_overlap(phase, date_offset_s, max_attempts):
    victims = start_victims()
    attacker = [sys.executable, "/tmp/repro.d/attacker.py", LOCK_PATH, str(date_offset_s)]
    for attempt in range(1, max_attempts + 1):
        run = subprocess.run(attacker, stdout=subprocess.PIPE, text=True, check=True,
                             user="attacker", group="attacker", extra_groups=[])
        print(f"{phase} attempt {attempt}: {run.stdout.strip()}", flush=True)
        unlinked_at = float(run.stdout.split("unlinked_at=")[1])
        time.sleep(0.4)  # a hold lasts 0.3 s: whoever entered after the unlink has logged it by now

        # A hold entered within 1 ms of the unlink can also come from a separate flaw in break_lock_file (see the
        # report), so those are left out. time.monotonic() is one clock for every process on the machine.
        holds = holds_entered_after(unlinked_at + 0.001)
        overlaps = [(first, second) for first, second in zip(holds, holds[1:])
                    if second["entered"] < first["exited"]]
        if overlaps:
            break
    for victim in victims:
        victim.kill()
        victim.wait()
    return overlaps


# control: the attacker's file is dated an hour after the tick in which it is unlinked
control = attack_until_overlap("CONTROL", date_offset_s=3600, max_attempts=20)
# attack: the same file dated at that tick, i.e. with the mtime a victim's marker created in that tick gets
observed = attack_until_overlap("OBSERVED", date_offset_s=0, max_attempts=250)

# check: no two victims may ever be inside the lock at once
for phase, overlaps in [("CONTROL", control), ("OBSERVED", observed)]:
    print(f"{phase}: {len(overlaps)} time(s) two victims inside the lock at once")
    for first, second in overlaps:
        print(f"{phase}:   {first['line']}")
        print(f"{phase}:   {second['line']}")
print("BUG" if observed and not control else "OK")
```

**`repro.d/attacker.py`**

```python
#!/usr/bin/env python3
import os
import random
import sys
import time

lock_path, date_offset_s = sys.argv[1], int(sys.argv[2])

CLOCK_REALTIME_COARSE = 5  # <linux/time.h>; the kernel stamps new files from it, and it moves once per timer tick
tick_ns = round(time.clock_getres(CLOCK_REALTIME_COARSE) * 1e9)

# take the lock path the moment it is free, like any contender
while True:
    try:
        fd = os.open(lock_path, os.O_CREAT | os.O_EXCL | os.O_WRONLY, 0o644)
        break
    except FileExistsError:
        time.sleep(0.002)

# Left empty for longer than the 2 s filelock gives an unparsable marker. The victims poll every 50 ms: the random
# part makes some attempts free the path just before one of their polls.
park_s = random.uniform(2.2, 2.25)
release_tick = time.clock_gettime_ns(CLOCK_REALTIME_COARSE) + round(park_s * 1e9 / tick_ns) * tick_ns
mtime_ns = release_tick + date_offset_s * 10**9
os.utime(fd, ns=(mtime_ns, mtime_ns))
inode = os.fstat(fd).st_ino
os.close(fd)

time.sleep(park_s - 0.05)
while time.clock_gettime_ns(CLOCK_REALTIME_COARSE) < release_tick:
    pass
os.unlink(lock_path)  # a marker created before the next tick gets mtime == release_tick and, on ext4, this inode
unlinked_at = time.monotonic()
time.sleep(0.1)  # exiting right away keeps a CPU busy during the victims' polls, and overlaps get much rarer
print(f"inode={inode} mtime_ns={mtime_ns} unlinked_in_tick={release_tick} unlinked_at={unlinked_at}")
```

**`repro.d/victim.py`**

```python
#!/usr/bin/env python3
import os
import sys
import time

from filelock import SoftFileLock

lock = SoftFileLock(sys.argv[1])
while True:
    with lock:
        entered = time.monotonic()
        time.sleep(0.3)  # work on whatever the lock protects
        print(f"pid={os.getpid()} entered={entered} exited={time.monotonic()} is_locked={lock.is_locked}", flush=True)
    time.sleep(0.05)
```

## Attack sequence

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
    participant X as other local user
    participant P as lock path (sticky dir, ext4, 4 ms clock ticks)
    participant S as process S of the lock user (waiting)
    participant F as process F of the lock user
    X->>P: create empty file, inode I, utime to future tick T
    S->>P: poll: empty file, key (T, I), watch starts
    Note over S: after 2 s each poll calls break_lock_file, rename gets EPERM, error swallowed, watch keeps counting
    rect rgb(255, 214, 214)
        X->>P: at tick T: unlink own file, I is free
        F->>P: O_EXCL create in tick T: inode I, mtime T, record not yet written
        S->>P: poll: empty file, key (T, I) seen for 2.2 s: break_lock_file(T, I) renames and unlinks F's marker
        F->>P: writes record into the unlinked inode, acquire() returns
        Note over S,F: the path is empty, the next contender creates a marker: two holders, no error
    end
```

## Evidence

The scanner's reproducer runs ten copies of a default-option `SoftFileLock` program (0.3 s of work per hold, 50 ms between holds) as user `victim` in a root-owned `1777` directory on overlayfs over ext4 (Linux 6.1, CPython 3.14). A program running as user `attacker` waits until the lock path is free, creates an empty file there, dates it to a coarse-clock tick 2.2 to 2.25 s ahead, and unlinks it when `CLOCK_REALTIME_COARSE` reaches that tick. Control attempts date the file an hour after the unlink tick (20 attempts, 0 overlaps); the other attempts date it at that tick.

In four runs the overlap came after 9, 12, 27 and 20 attempts. Each showed the hold lines of two `victim` processes overlapping in time with `is_locked=True`, for example `pid=217 entered=241.295272609 exited=241.59542327` and `pid=216 entered=241.295518489 exited=241.595641553`. 40 of 650 attempts over seven runs ended this way, none with the file dated 4 ms earlier (100 attempts) or an hour later (150). A stepped run (one process stalled 0.2 s between creating its marker and writing its record, one waiting contender) deleted the fresh marker in 3 of 3 trials with the matching date and 0 of 5 with other dates.

Our review ran the reproducer over a loop-mounted ext4 `/tmp` (the host's btrfs does not hand a freed number back) with inode reuse confirmed (inode 18 reused on every attempt, `--cpus 2`). 0 of 250 attempts fired on 4.2.0 in 802 s, as in the scanner-side triage, and 0 of 250 on the head of #843, so our run gives no evidence either way. The review confirmed that `utime` cannot set the file's change time. The classification follows from the cross-UID inode-reuse primitive verified in the stale-break race of the separate advisory and from the report's own runs.

## Impact

A local user who can create a file in a soft lock's directory, a sticky directory such as `/tmp` included, gets two processes of another user to hold the same `SoftFileLock` at once (`MarkerSoftFileLock` too, by the shared code). Neither process learns of the overlap, so both modify the data the lock protects. The other user has no simpler way to get this: in the sticky directory its `unlink`, `rename`, `open(..., "w")` and `utime` on a marker of the lock user all fail, and deleting its own file only frees the lock. For `SoftFileLease` the effect is a live, refreshed claim taken after milliseconds instead of after `lease_duration` without a refresh. The holder learns of it one heartbeat later, or not at all if it releases first. Not affected: releases before 4.1.0, filesystems that do not reuse inode numbers at once (tmpfs, btrfs), and a lock with a single contender.

## Workarounds

Keep soft locks in a directory other users cannot create files in (a `0700` directory of the lock's user) rather than a shared sticky directory, or put the lock directory on tmpfs, which does not reuse inode numbers. Where the native `FileLock` works (local ext4 with `flock`), prefer it over `SoftFileLock`. Raise `poll_interval` so fewer waiters bunch inside one clock tick; this lowers the hit rate but does not close the window.

## Patched version

4.2.1.

Fix: https://github.com/tox-dev/filelock/pull/843

items.title: filelock: ReadWriteLock on Windows acts on SQLite side files another local user places beside its database
items.description:
On Windows, `ReadWriteLock` and `AsyncReadWriteLock` (the SQLite-backed reader/writer lock) connect SQLite to the lock database by its path, in every directory. SQLite derives three side files from that path: `<database>-journal`, the rollback journal (pages saved to undo an interrupted write); `<database>-wal`, the write-ahead log (changes kept outside the main file); and `<database>-shm`, the shared-memory index of the WAL. SQLite acts on whichever of these it finds beside the database before the lock runs any statement. Another local account that can create files in the database's directory, but not delete files of other accounts there, places such a side file beside the database and denies everyone `DELETE` on it, which a file's creator may do. `C:\Windows\Temp` (the temporary directory of services, granting `BUILTIN\Users` create but not delete) and `C:\Users\Public` are such directories.

With a `-wal` in place, every `read_lock()` and `write_lock()` of the user running the lock (below: the lock user) raises `sqlite3.OperationalError: disk I/O error` at once, whatever `timeout` says, until that account removes its file; the lock user cannot. With a `-journal` beside a lock database that holds a table, SQLite replays the journal and deletes the file the journal names, a file of the lock user, and the acquire reports success. Affected versions are filelock 3.20.4 through 4.2.0 on Windows. The maintainers found this while reviewing the fix for the POSIX form of the defect, GHSA-v4x8-3wr5-3wq8, whose text says "Windows does not take this path" (review round 4, finding F2 of set D). It is not among the findings of the report Anthropic's OSS Scanner sent on 15 October 2026.

## Severity

**CVSS 3.1 `CVSS:3.1/AV:L/AC:L/PR:L/UI:N/S:U/C:N/I:N/A:L` scores 3.3 (Low).**

`AV:L` (local): the other account needs a logon on the same host. `AC:L` (low attack complexity): create one file beside the database and set its ACL (access control list); no race, and the other account can place the file days earlier. `PR:L` (low privileges): an ordinary account that can create files in the directory is enough. `UI:N` (no user interaction). `S:U` (scope unchanged). `C:N` (no confidentiality impact): the other account learns nothing. `I:N` (no integrity impact in the scored variant): see the scoring note. `A:L` (partial availability impact): every acquire fails with an exception that `Timeout` handlers do not catch, until the other account removes its file; no crash, and the lock's own data is not changed.

Scoring note. The deletion variant reads `CVSS:3.1/AV:L/AC:H/PR:L/UI:N/S:U/C:N/I:L/A:L` (3.6): `I:L` because the lock user's process deletes one file the journal names, `AC:H` because it needs a lock database that holds a table, which filelock does not create, and a journal the lock user can open for writing. The lower-reading rule of this advisory set scores the variant that reaches every `ReadWriteLock` on Windows in such a directory, 3.3, and describes the deletion variant under Mechanism. Classification from the review: **security** (another account), availability for the scored variant.

## Scope and preconditions

- Platform and classes: Windows only. `ReadWriteLock` and `AsyncReadWriteLock`, both of which connect through `_connect`. On Linux and macOS the lock takes other routes, covered by GHSA-v4x8-3wr5-3wq8.
- Directory: one where another account can create files but cannot delete the lock user's. `C:\Windows\Temp` carries `BUILTIN\Users:(CI)(S,WD,AD,X)` (create file and create subdirectory, no delete child); `C:\Users\Public` and any directory with such an entry qualify. A directory only the lock user can write, such as `%LOCALAPPDATA%` or the per-user temporary directory, is not affected.
- The other account creates `<database>-wal`, grants everyone modify and denies everyone `DELETE` on it. A file's creator may set both. The lock user can open and read the file but not delete it.
- Deletion variant: the lock database holds at least one table (filelock creates an empty database, and the review's reproducer has the lock account create the table), and the other account's `<database>-journal` grants the lock account modify rights. The journal's tail names a file the lock user can delete.
- What the lock user sees: `write_lock(timeout=1)` raised `sqlite3.OperationalError: disk I/O error` with the undeletable `-wal` in place; with the writable journal the acquire succeeded and the named file was gone; with an undeletable journal every acquire raised `sqlite3.OperationalError: unable to open database file`.
- The documentation at the scanned commit states "the lock directory must not be writable by untrusted users" for `WindowsFileLock`, in its symlink paragraph; the `ReadWriteLock` documentation names no directory requirement on Windows.

## Affected code

Scanned commit `b831496b0273`: the [Windows branch of `_connect`](https://github.com/tox-dev/filelock/blob/b831496b0273ecd11bf02b8d080ca8b673a538c1/src/filelock/_read_write.py#L951-L965) checks the database through a handle and then calls `sqlite3.connect(database, ...)` with the path. [`_open_lock_database`](https://github.com/tox-dev/filelock/blob/b831496b0273ecd11bf02b8d080ca8b673a538c1/src/filelock/_read_write.py#L1079-L1091) and [`_raise_if_wal`](https://github.com/tox-dev/filelock/blob/b831496b0273ecd11bf02b8d080ca8b673a538c1/src/filelock/_read_write.py#L1094-L1101) inspect that handle, not the side files. The first statement is [`PRAGMA busy_timeout=...; PRAGMA journal_mode=MEMORY;` at L816](https://github.com/tox-dev/filelock/blob/b831496b0273ecd11bf02b8d080ca8b673a538c1/src/filelock/_read_write.py#L816). [`_do_acquire_inner` at L763](https://github.com/tox-dev/filelock/blob/b831496b0273ecd11bf02b8d080ca8b673a538c1/src/filelock/_read_write.py#L763) turns only `"database is locked"` into `Timeout`; any other `sqlite3.OperationalError` leaves the acquire.

## Introduced

[cfd4446](https://github.com/tox-dev/filelock/commit/cfd4446) "feat(lock): add SQLite-based ReadWriteLock" ([#399](https://github.com/tox-dev/filelock/pull/399), 2026-02-12), first tag 3.20.4 (verified with `git tag --contains`), passed the lock path to `sqlite3.connect` on every platform. The Linux descriptor route (4.0.9) and the macOS hard-link route (4.1.1) did not change Windows, where the connect has been by name in every release since. The reproducer ran against the head of PR #834 at `1f9e415`, whose Windows branch of `_connect` is the same code as at `b831496b0273`.

## Mechanism

`_connect` on Windows opens the database with `_open_non_reparse_fd`, checks through that handle that the file is a regular file, not a reparse point, and that its header does not declare WAL mode, and keeps the handle open while `sqlite3.connect(database)` opens the same name. The check covers the database, not the names beside it. On the first statement, `PRAGMA journal_mode=MEMORY`, SQLite takes its first lock on the database and looks for `<database>-wal`. A non-empty `-wal` beside a database that is not in WAL mode is a leftover SQLite deletes. The other account's file denies `DELETE`, so the pragma raises `SQLITE_IOERR_DELETE`, which reaches the caller as `sqlite3.OperationalError: disk I/O error`. `_do_acquire_inner` converts only "database is locked" into `Timeout`, so `acquire_read()`, `acquire_write()` and the async forms raise at once, on every call, until the file is gone. The lock user has no right to delete it.

The journal variant needs a database with content. Beside a non-empty database SQLite treats a `<database>-journal` with a valid header as hot (left by an interrupted write) and replays it before the first statement runs. The review's journal is 46 bytes: a file path, its 4-byte length, the 4-byte sum of its bytes and SQLite's journal magic. That tail names a super-journal, and recovery ends by deleting the file it names. The lock user's `write_lock()` therefore deletes one file the other account chose, provided the lock user can delete it, and returns without error. SQLite opens a hot journal for writing, so the other account's journal must grant the lock account modify rights; a read-only journal makes every acquire raise `sqlite3.OperationalError: unable to open database file` instead. GHSA-v4x8-3wr5-3wq8 describes the same side-file behavior on POSIX, where the sticky bit plays the part the directory ACL plays here.

## Reproduction

The review's reproducer, quoted as received except for the second account's password on line 2, replaced by `<password>`. It ran on a Windows 11 VM (NTFS, CPython 3.14, SQLite 3.53.1) against the head of PR #834 at `1f9e415`, as the administrator account `bernat`, which stands in for the other account that creates the side files; the lock account is `fltester`, a member of `Users`, whose database lives in `C:\Windows\Temp`.

**`win_two_accounts.py`**

```python
# Run from /tmp/claude-1000/-home-bernat-git-filelock-filelock-main/3ccf38c2-14f9-4acc-a05f-18230504d7cd/scratchpad/review4/D/834 (the script is staged there):
#   winvm up && winvm sync && winvm run "python3.14 -I win_two_accounts.py . fltester '<password>'"
# which runs, as the administrator account on the VM:
#   python3.14 -I win_two_accounts.py <worktree> <second-user> <password>
# The second (non-administrator) account is the lock user. Its database lives in C:\Windows\Temp, where every account
# may create files but not delete another account's. This administrator account stands in for the other account that
# plants SQLite side files there: it creates them, grants everyone read, and denies everyone delete, all of which the
# file's creator may do.
import ctypes
import os
import pathlib
import sqlite3
import struct
import subprocess
import sys
from ctypes import wintypes

sys.path.insert(0, sys.argv[1] + "/src")
from filelock import ReadWriteLock

user, password = sys.argv[2], sys.argv[3]
base = pathlib.Path(os.environ["SYSTEMROOT"]) / "Temp"
icacls = os.path.join(os.environ["SYSTEMROOT"], "System32", "icacls.exe")
tag = f"rw834-{os.getpid()}"
advapi32 = ctypes.WinDLL("advapi32", use_last_error=True)
advapi32.LogonUserW.argtypes = [wintypes.LPCWSTR, wintypes.LPCWSTR, wintypes.LPCWSTR, wintypes.DWORD, wintypes.DWORD, ctypes.POINTER(wintypes.HANDLE)]
advapi32.GetUserNameW.argtypes = [wintypes.LPWSTR, ctypes.POINTER(wintypes.DWORD)]
token = wintypes.HANDLE()
if not advapi32.LogonUserW(user, ".", password, 3, 0, ctypes.byref(token)):
    raise ctypes.WinError(ctypes.get_last_error())


def current_user() -> str:
    size = wintypes.DWORD(256)
    buffer = ctypes.create_unicode_buffer(size.value)
    advapi32.GetUserNameW(buffer, ctypes.byref(size))
    return buffer.value


def as_lock_user(action):
    if not advapi32.ImpersonateLoggedOnUser(token):
        raise ctypes.WinError(ctypes.get_last_error())
    try:
        return action()
    finally:
        advapi32.RevertToSelf()


def plant(path: pathlib.Path, data: bytes, *, deletable: bool) -> None:
    path.write_bytes(data)
    subprocess.run([icacls, str(path), "/grant", "*S-1-1-0:(M)"], check=True, capture_output=True)
    if not deletable:
        subprocess.run([icacls, str(path), "/deny", "*S-1-1-0:(D)"], check=True, capture_output=True)


def acquire(db: pathlib.Path) -> str:
    try:
        with ReadWriteLock(db, is_singleton=False).write_lock(timeout=1):
            pass
    except Exception as error:
        return f"acquire failed: {type(error).__name__}: {error}"
    return "acquired"


def hot_journal(super_journal: pathlib.Path) -> bytes:
    name = os.fsencode(str(super_journal))
    return name + struct.pack(">II", len(name), sum(name)) + bytes.fromhex("d9d505f920a163d7")


print("planting account:", current_user(), "| lock account:", as_lock_user(current_user))

db = base / f"{tag}-empty.db"
as_lock_user(lambda: db.touch())
plant(pathlib.Path(f"{db}-wal"), b"\0" * 32, deletable=False)
print("empty database, undeletable -wal:", as_lock_user(lambda: acquire(db)), "| -wal still exists:", pathlib.Path(f"{db}-wal").exists())

for deletable in (True, False):
    db = base / f"{tag}-tables-{deletable}.db"
    notes = base / f"{tag}-notes-{deletable}.txt"

    def prepare() -> None:
        with sqlite3.connect(db) as connection:
            connection.execute("CREATE TABLE application (value)")
        connection.close()
        notes.write_text("keep")

    as_lock_user(prepare)
    plant(pathlib.Path(f"{db}-journal"), hot_journal(notes), deletable=deletable)
    print(f"database with a table, {'deletable' if deletable else 'undeletable'} -journal naming the lock account's file:",
          as_lock_user(lambda: acquire(db)), "| named file still exists:", notes.exists(), "| -journal still exists:", pathlib.Path(f"{db}-journal").exists())
```

Recorded output on the VM:

```text
planting account: bernat | lock account: fltester
empty database, undeletable -wal: acquire failed: OperationalError: disk I/O error | -wal still exists: True
database with a table, deletable -journal naming the lock account's file: acquired | named file still exists: False | -journal still exists: False
database with a table, undeletable -journal naming the lock account's file: acquire failed: OperationalError: unable to open database file | named file still exists: True | -journal still exists: True
```

## Failure sequence

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    P["other account: create lock.db-wal (or lock.db-journal) beside lock.db in C:/Windows/Temp, grant everyone modify, deny everyone DELETE"] --> C["lock user: ReadWriteLock(lock.db).write_lock(timeout=1)"]
    C --> O["_open_lock_database checks the handle: regular file, no reparse point, header not WAL"]
    O --> S["sqlite3.connect(lock.db) by path, then PRAGMA journal_mode=MEMORY"]
    S -- "empty database, undeletable -wal" --> E1["SQLite cannot delete the leftover -wal: OperationalError disk I/O error on every acquire, timeout not consulted"]
    S -- "database with a table, writable -journal" --> E2["SQLite treats the journal as hot, replays it and deletes the file its tail names, acquire succeeds"]
    S -- "database with a table, read-only -journal" --> E3["OperationalError unable to open database file on every acquire"]
    classDef ok fill:#d8f3dc,stroke:#2d6a4f,color:#1b4332;
    classDef bad fill:#ffd6d6,stroke:#c1121f,color:#5c0000;
    classDef info fill:#cfe4ff,stroke:#1f6feb,color:#0b1f3a;
    class P,C,O,S info;
    class E1,E2,E3 bad;
```

## Evidence

The reproducer printed the three lines above on the VM: the undeletable `-wal` beside an empty database made `write_lock(timeout=1)` fail with `OperationalError: disk I/O error` and left the file in place; the writable journal beside a database with one table let the acquire succeed while the file the journal named, created by the lock account with the content `keep`, was gone along with the journal; the read-only journal made the acquire fail with `OperationalError: unable to open database file` and left both files. The review notes that the Windows branch of `_connect` is unchanged since #399, so the behavior is the same at `b831496b0273` and in 4.2.0. The scanner and the maintainers measured the same side-file effects on Linux for GHSA-v4x8-3wr5-3wq8.

## Impact

In a directory such as `C:\Windows\Temp`, another local account turns every `read_lock()` and `write_lock()` on a `ReadWriteLock` database into an immediate `sqlite3.OperationalError`, for as long as its file stays. Callers that handle `Timeout` or `OSError` do not catch it, and the lock user cannot remove the file. With a lock database that holds a table and a journal the lock user can write, the lock user's process deletes one file of the other account's choosing, among the files the lock user may delete, and the acquire reports success. The lock's own database is not changed, nothing is read, and mutual exclusion between processes that acquire the lock holds.

## Workarounds

- Keep the `ReadWriteLock` database in a directory other accounts cannot create files in: `%LOCALAPPDATA%`, the per-user temporary directory (`%TEMP%` of a user session), or a directory with inheritance removed and only the owner, `SYSTEM` and `Administrators` granted. `C:\Windows\Temp` and `C:\Users\Public` do not qualify.
- Treat `sqlite3.OperationalError: disk I/O error` on every acquire as a foreign `<database>-wal` beside the database, which only its creator or an administrator can remove.

## Patched version

4.2.1.

Fix: https://github.com/tox-dev/filelock/pull/854

Found by the maintainers while reviewing the fix for the POSIX form of this defect, GHSA-v4x8-3wr5-3wq8, reported by Anthropic's OSS Scanner on 15 October 2026 (review round 4, set D, finding F2).

Traefik before 2.11.46, 3.x before 3.6.17, and 3.7.0 lack namespace validation for Ingress and Service annotations in the Kubernetes Ingress provider, allowing references to Middlewares, ServersTransports, and TLSOptions in other namespaces. Attackers able to create or update Ingress or Service resources in one namespace can set router.middlewares or service.serverstransport annotations to obtain another tenant's injected credentials or reuse its client certificates, bypassing namespace-based tenant isolation.

items.title: filelock: On Windows an oplock on a soft lock's marker holds SoftFileLock.acquire() past its timeout and blocks the stale break
items.description:
On Windows the soft locks (`SoftFileLock`, `MarkerSoftFileLock`, `SoftFileLease`, their async forms, and a `FileLock` that fell back to a soft lock) read their marker by path. The marker is the lock file whose presence says a process holds the lock. Each `acquire()` attempt that finds a marker opens it with `os.open` to read the holder's process id, and the lock renames and deletes a marker it judges stale, by path. On Windows each of these calls waits for an oplock. An oplock (opportunistic lock) is a request by a process that holds a handle on a file to be told before another process opens, renames or deletes that file; the other process waits until the holder answers the break or closes its handle.

Another local account that can open the marker for reading can take a Level 1 oplock on it while no process holds it open, and leave the break unanswered. Every `acquire()` by the user running the lock (below: the lock user) then waits inside the open, past its `timeout`, `blocking=False` and `cancel_check`, and a stale marker under that oplock is not broken. Mutual exclusion holds and the lock touches no other file. Affected versions are filelock 3.22.0 through 4.2.0 on Windows. The maintainers found this while reviewing the fix for the report Anthropic's OSS Scanner sent on 15 October 2026 (review round 4, finding F4); it is not among the scanner's findings.

## Severity

**CVSS 3.1 `CVSS:3.1/AV:L/AC:H/PR:L/UI:N/S:U/C:N/I:N/A:L` scores 2.5 (Low).**

`AV:L` (local): the other account needs a logon on the same host. `AC:H` (high attack complexity): Windows grants a Level 1 or batch oplock only to the sole open handle on a file, so the marker must have no holder handle when the other account asks. That account cannot bring this about; it waits for a holder that died, closed its descriptor, or left a marker past its `lifetime`. `PR:L` (low privileges): an ordinary account with read access to the marker through the directory's inherited ACL (access control list). `UI:N` (no user interaction). `S:U` (scope unchanged). `C:N` and `I:N`: that account can read the marker's content (process id and host name) anyway, and mutual exclusion holds. `A:L` (partial availability impact): one thread, or the event loop with `run_in_executor=False`, waits until the holder answers; 10 s per attempt in the two-account runs, no crash. Metrics in doubt take the lower reading.

Classification from the review: **security, conditional** on an unheld marker that another account can open.

## Scope and preconditions

- Platform and classes: Windows only. `SoftFileLock`, `MarkerSoftFileLock`, `SoftFileLease`, `AsyncSoftFileLock` and the other async soft locks, and `FileLock` after its `ENOSYS` fallback to a soft lock. `WindowsFileLock` opens its lock file on a separate code path that this advisory does not cover.
- Marker access: the soft locks create the marker with `os.open`, which on Windows applies no more of `mode` than the read-only attribute (GHSA-8mx5-7m5m-r77g). The marker carries the lock directory's inheritable entries. Another account that those entries grant read access to new files can open the marker with a read handle that shares read, write and delete.
- Unheld marker: no handle may be open on the marker when the other account requests the oplock. That is a holder that died and left its marker, a holder that closed its descriptor, or a marker whose `lifetime` has passed. While the holder keeps its handle, the request fails.
- Holder behavior: the other account requests the oplock through an overlapped `DeviceIoControl` and never acknowledges the break. Windows cancels a thread's pending request when the thread exits, so the holder thread stays alive. A same-account process that answers slowly, such as an indexer, has the same effect for its answer time.
- What the lock user sees: `SoftFileLock.acquire(timeout=1)` returned `Timeout` after 10.02 s with the second account's handle. In the same-account probe `os.open` with `O_RDONLY` was still running after 15 s and returned once the holder closed. The retry loop consults `timeout`, `blocking=False` and `cancel_check` between attempts only. With `AsyncSoftFileLock(run_in_executor=False)` the event loop waits.
- Stale break: `break_lock_file` renames and unlinks by path. Both calls wait in the same way, so a stale marker under such an oplock stays, and no process acquires the lock until the holder closes.
- Not affected: mutual exclusion, and the lock reads, writes and deletes no file other than the marker.

## Affected code

Scanned commit `b831496b0273`: the [`os.open` in `_read_lock_file`](https://github.com/tox-dev/filelock/blob/b831496b0273ecd11bf02b8d080ca8b673a538c1/src/filelock/_soft.py#L323) ([function](https://github.com/tox-dev/filelock/blob/b831496b0273ecd11bf02b8d080ca8b673a538c1/src/filelock/_soft.py#L312-L335)), called from [`_try_break_stale_lock`](https://github.com/tox-dev/filelock/blob/b831496b0273ecd11bf02b8d080ca8b673a538c1/src/filelock/_soft.py#L107-L123) on every attempt that finds a marker, and from [`_unprobeable_holder`](https://github.com/tox-dev/filelock/blob/b831496b0273ecd11bf02b8d080ca8b673a538c1/src/filelock/_soft.py#L137), [`pid`](https://github.com/tox-dev/filelock/blob/b831496b0273ecd11bf02b8d080ca8b673a538c1/src/filelock/_soft.py#L164) and [`is_lock_held_by_us`](https://github.com/tox-dev/filelock/blob/b831496b0273ecd11bf02b8d080ca8b673a538c1/src/filelock/_soft.py#L179). [`break_lock_file`](https://github.com/tox-dev/filelock/blob/b831496b0273ecd11bf02b8d080ca8b673a538c1/src/filelock/_util.py#L84-L122) renames at L116 and unlinks at L118 and L122, by path. [`_poll_until_acquired`](https://github.com/tox-dev/filelock/blob/b831496b0273ecd11bf02b8d080ca8b673a538c1/src/filelock/_api.py#L1378-L1408) and [`_check_give_up`](https://github.com/tox-dev/filelock/blob/b831496b0273ecd11bf02b8d080ca8b673a538c1/src/filelock/_api.py#L1590-L1608) test the deadline, `blocking` and `cancel_check` only between attempts.

## Introduced

[e35c3af](https://github.com/tox-dev/filelock/commit/e35c3af) "feat(soft): detect and break stale locks" ([#476](https://github.com/tox-dev/filelock/pull/476), 2026-02-13), first tag 3.22.0 (verified with `git tag --contains`). Before it a soft lock created its marker with `O_CREAT | O_EXCL` and never opened an existing one. #476 read the marker on Windows through `CreateFileW` and broke a stale one with `Path.rename` and `Path.unlink`. These wait for an oplock as `os.open` does, because none of them passes `FILE_COMPLETE_IF_OPLOCKED`, an `NtCreateFile` option that returns instead of waiting. The read became the `os.open` in `_read_lock_file` with [bfbfa76](https://github.com/tox-dev/filelock/commit/bfbfa76) ([#548](https://github.com/tox-dev/filelock/pull/548), 3.29.1) and the break moved into `break_lock_file` with [d244c6d](https://github.com/tox-dev/filelock/commit/d244c6d) ([#551](https://github.com/tox-dev/filelock/pull/551), 3.29.2); the by-path calls stayed.

## Mechanism

Each attempt of `_acquire` first calls `os.open(path, O_WRONLY | O_CREAT | O_EXCL)`. On an existing marker that fails with `EEXIST` (or `EACCES` on Windows) at once; the same-account probe shows the failed exclusive create returning at once under an oplock too. `_acquire` then calls `_try_break_stale_lock`, which calls `_read_lock_file`: `os.lstat`, then `os.open(path, O_RDONLY | O_NOFOLLOW | O_NONBLOCK)`. On Windows `O_NOFOLLOW` and `O_NONBLOCK` do not exist (the code reads them with `getattr(os, ..., 0)`), and `os.open` calls `CreateFileW`. When another handle holds a Level 1 or batch oplock on the file, that call sends the holder a break request and returns only when the holder acknowledges it or closes its handle. `_check_give_up` tests the deadline after the attempt returns, so the wait overruns `timeout`, `blocking=False` and `cancel_check` by its length. Once the open returns, the attempt ends and `_check_give_up` raises `Timeout`, because the deadline has passed.

A marker whose holder is gone takes the second path. `break_lock_file` renames it to a break name and unlinks it, by path. On Windows the rename and the delete open the file with delete access, which breaks a Level 1 or batch oplock the same way; the same-account probe shows `os.rename` and `os.unlink` still running after 15 s and returning once the holder closed. The `lifetime` break at L123 runs the same function. A stale marker under such an oplock is therefore not removed, and every attempt by every process waits inside the read. The other account can request the oplock again as soon as the lock user's handle closes, between two attempts or two `acquire()` calls, as in the Linux lease case of GHSA-7hmp-gf99-57hx. Nothing in the retry loop bounds this wait.

## Reproduction

The review's reproducers, quoted as received. `oplock_vm.py` section `[2]` is this finding; sections `[1a]` and `[1b]` belong to the `release()` advisory. `oplock_semantics_vm.py` is the same-account probe of which path operations wait. They ran on a Windows 11 VM (NTFS, CPython 3.14.8) against the head of PR #835 at `3e4c5ef`, where `_read_lock_file` and `break_lock_file` are the same code as at `b831496b0273` apart from import changes. The second account `fltester` is a member of `Users`; the directory grants it `(OI)(CI)(M)`.

**`oplock_vm.py`**

```python
"""
Windows oplock checks beyond the lock-file open PR #835 changes: release() and the soft locks' marker read.

Run on the VM (PowerShell, from the synced worktree, with the fltester account present):
  C:\\venvs\\rev4F\\Scripts\\python.exe oplock_vm.py fltester '<password>' C:\\tmp\\rev4F-oplock

[1] A second account keeps requesting a Level 1 oplock on the lock file through a read handle that shares delete.
    WindowsFileLock._release closes its handle and then unlinks by path; an oplock granted in between makes the
    DeleteFileW inside os.unlink wait for the holder's acknowledgement. [1a] races the close-to-unlink window as is;
    [1b] widens that window to 200 ms with a patched os.unlink so the grant lands inside it.
[2] A second account holds a Level 1 oplock on a soft-lock marker whose holder is alive. SoftFileLock.acquire reads the
    marker through os.open, which waits for the acknowledgement, past timeout=1.

A thread that exits has its pending oplock request cancelled, so every holder thread stays alive until the end.

import os
import subprocess
import sys
import threading
import time
from ctypes import wintypes

    ctypes.POINTER(wintypes.HANDLE),
]
kernel32.CreateFileW.restype = kernel32.CreateEventW.restype = wintypes.HANDLE
kernel32.CreateFileW.argtypes = [
    wintypes.LPCWSTR,
    wintypes.DWORD,
    wintypes.DWORD,
    ctypes.c_void_p,
    wintypes.DWORD,
    wintypes.DWORD,
    wintypes.HANDLE,

class Overlapped(ctypes.Structure):

        ("Internal", ctypes.c_void_p),
        ("InternalHigh", ctypes.c_void_p),
        ("Offset", wintypes.DWORD),
        ("OffsetHigh", wintypes.DWORD),
        ("hEvent", wintypes.HANDLE),
    )


kernel32.DeviceIoControl.argtypes = [
    wintypes.HANDLE,
    wintypes.DWORD,
    ctypes.c_void_p,
    wintypes.DWORD,
    ctypes.c_void_p,
    wintypes.DWORD,
    ctypes.c_void_p,
    ctypes.POINTER(Overlapped),

kernel32.CloseHandle.argtypes = [wintypes.HANDLE]
kernel32.WaitForSingleObject.argtypes = [wintypes.HANDLE, wintypes.DWORD]

SHARE_ALL = 0x7
OPEN_EXISTING = 3
FLAG_OVERLAPPED = 0x40000000
INVALID_HANDLE = wintypes.HANDLE(-1).value
FSCTL_REQUEST_OPLOCK_LEVEL_1 = 0x00090000
ERROR_IO_PENDING = 997
hold = threading.Event()
real_unlink = os.unlink


def impersonate() -> None:
    token = wintypes.HANDLE()
    if not advapi32.LogonUserW(user, ".", password, 3, 0, ctypes.byref(token)):
        raise ctypes.WinError(ctypes.get_last_error())

def release_under_oplock_requests(label: str, lock_path: str, cycles: int) -> bool:
    stop = threading.Event()
    granted_box: list[tuple[int, Overlapped]] = []

    def spinner() -> None:
        impersonate()
        while not stop.is_set():
            if (granted := request_level1(lock_path)) is not None:
                granted_box.append(granted)
                hold.wait()
                return

    releasing = threading.Event()
    release_durations: list[float] = []

    def owner() -> None:
        # thread_local locks release only on the acquiring thread, so acquire and release stay on this one
        for _ in range(cycles):
            lock = FileLock(lock_path, is_singleton=False)
            lock.acquire(timeout=5)
            started = time.monotonic()
            releasing.set()
            lock.release()
            releasing.clear()
            release_durations.append(time.monotonic() - started)
            if granted_box:
                return

    holder = threading.Thread(target=spinner, daemon=True)
    holder.start()
    owner_thread = threading.Thread(target=owner, daemon=True)
    owner_thread.start()
    owner_thread.join(60)
    stalled = owner_thread.is_alive() and releasing.is_set()
    stop.set()
    longest = max(release_durations, default=0.0) * 1000
    print(f"  {label}: oplock granted: {bool(granted_box)}; cycles run: {len(release_durations)}; longest release: {longest:.1f} ms")
    if stalled:
        print("  release() still running after 60 s while the oplock holder has not answered the break")
        if granted_box:
            drop(granted_box[0])
        owner_thread.join(10)
        print(f"  release() returned after the holder closed its handle: {not owner_thread.is_alive()}")
    return stalled
```

## Failure sequence

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
    participant A as other local account
    participant M as soft.lock marker, no handle open
    participant L as lock user: SoftFileLock(path).acquire(timeout=1)
    participant W as Windows (NTFS)

    L->>W: os.open(soft.lock, O_CREAT|O_EXCL) fails with EEXIST at once
    L->>W: os.lstat(soft.lock) regular file
    rect rgb(255, 214, 214)
        L->>W: os.open(soft.lock, O_RDONLY) inside _read_lock_file
        Note over L,W: CreateFileW asks A to break the oplock and waits#59; the 1 s deadline, blocking=False and cancel_check are not consulted
        W-->>L: handle after 10.02 s (two-account run), or when A closes (same-account probe)
    end
    L->>L: _check_give_up: past the deadline, raise Timeout after 10.02 s
    Note over A,M: a stale marker takes the same wait in Path.rename and Path.unlink, so it is not broken
```

## Evidence

Section `[2]` of `oplock_vm.py` acquired `soft.lock` as the test account, closed the holder's descriptor so the marker stayed with a live process id and no open handle, took a Level 1 oplock through the second account's read handle (`oplock granted: True`), and ran `SoftFileLock(marker, is_singleton=False).acquire(timeout=1)` on a thread. The call returned `Timeout` after 10.02 s, before the holder closed. The review did not establish what ends the wait at 10 s in the two-account runs; section `[1a]` of the same script, with the second account's handle, shows the same 10 s. In the same-account probe (`oplock_semantics_vm.py`) the open returned only when the holder closed, still running at 15 s. The probe also shows that the failed exclusive create and `os.utime` by path return at once, so the wait is in the read and the break, not in the create attempt.

## Impact

Each `acquire()` of a soft lock that finds a marker another account holds an oplock on runs past its `timeout`, `blocking=False` and `cancel_check` until the holder answers or closes, 10 s per attempt in the recorded two-account runs. A stale marker under that oplock is not broken, so no process acquires the lock while the holder keeps its handle. With `AsyncSoftFileLock(run_in_executor=False)` the wait is on the event loop thread and stops every task in the process; with the default executor one worker thread waits. The documentation names a soft lock as the option for network filesystems, after verification on the mount, and `FileLock` is a soft lock on builds without `fcntl` and after its `ENOSYS` fallback. Mutual exclusion is not affected and nothing other than the marker is read, written or deleted.

## Workarounds

- Keep soft-lock markers in a directory whose ACL grants other accounts no access to new files: a directory inside the user profile, or one with inheritance removed and only the owner, `SYSTEM` and `Administrators` granted (`icacls <dir> /inheritance:r /grant:r "<owner>:(OI)(CI)F" "SYSTEM:(OI)(CI)F" "Administrators:(OI)(CI)F"`). `mode` does not do this on Windows.
- Run `AsyncSoftFileLock` with the default executor rather than `run_in_executor=False`, so that only a worker thread waits.
- No `timeout`, `blocking` or `cancel_check` value bounds the wait.

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

irqchip/gic-v5: Immediately exec priority drop following activate

With GICv5 an interrupt of equal or lower priority cannot be signalled
until there has been a priority drop. This is done via the GIC CDEOI
system instruction. Once this has been executed, the hardware is able
to signal the next interrupt if there is one.

As all interrupts are programmed to have the same priority, no new
interrupts can be signalled until the priority drop has happened. This
can cause issues when, for example, an interrupt remains active while
a long running process takes place, such as when injecting a physical
interrupt into a guest VM in software.

The GICv5 driver has so far done the priority drop as part of
irq_eoi(), i.e., at the same time as deactivating the interrupt. This
means that any long running process (or VM) could block incoming
interrupts, effectively causing a denial of service for all other
interrupts.

Rather than doing the EOI as part of irq_eoi() (which the name would
suggest would be a good place for it), move it to happen immediately
after acknowledging an interrupt in the main GICv5 interrupt
handler. The deactivation of interrupts (GIC CDDI) remains implemented
as part of irq_eoi(), which means that the same interrupt cannot be
signalled a second time until deactivated by software.

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

drm/gma500: return errors from Oaktrail HDMI I2C reads

xfer_read() waits for the HDMI I2C transaction to reach
I2C_TRANSACTION_DONE, but it ignores both timeout and signal returns from
wait_for_completion_interruptible_timeout().  If the interrupt never
advances the transaction state, the loop can wait forever.

Return -ETIMEDOUT when the completion wait expires, propagate interrupted
waits, and make the I2C master_xfer callback return the first transfer
error instead of reporting a successful message count.

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

wifi: mac80211_hwsim: reject undersized HWSIM_ATTR_TX_INFO

hwsim_tx_info_frame_received_nl() casts the HWSIM_ATTR_TX_INFO payload
to a struct hwsim_tx_rate * and unconditionally reads
IEEE80211_TX_MAX_RATES entries (8 bytes) from it. The policy only bounds
the attribute from above (NLA_BINARY .len is a maximum) and the op sets
GENL_DONT_VALIDATE_STRICT, so a short or zero-length attribute is
accepted and the loop reads past the payload.

Require the exact length in the policy, so a malformed attribute is
rejected before the handler runs.

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

arm64: kprobes: Allow reentering kprobes while single-stepping

A kprobe can be hit while another kprobe is in KPROBE_HIT_SS state. This
can happen when tracing or perf code runs from the debug exception path
while the first kprobe is preparing or executing its out-of-line
single-step instruction.

Currently arm64 treats a kprobe hit in KPROBE_HIT_SS as unrecoverable,
the same as a hit in KPROBE_REENTER. This is too strict. A hit in
KPROBE_HIT_SS is still a one-level reentry and can be handled by saving
the current kprobe state and setting up single-step for the new probe,
just like reentry from KPROBE_HIT_ACTIVE or KPROBE_HIT_SSDONE.

The truly unrecoverable case is hitting another kprobe while already in
KPROBE_REENTER, because the reentry save area has already been consumed.

Move KPROBE_HIT_SS to the recoverable reentry cases and leave
KPROBE_REENTER as the unrecoverable nested reentry case.

This change also requires saving saved_irqflag in struct prev_kprobe.
When a nested kprobe calls kprobes_save_local_irqflag(), it overwrites
kcb->saved_irqflag with the currently masked DAIF value, losing the
outer kprobe's original DAIF state. Without this fix, when the outer
kprobe's single-step finishes, kprobes_restore_local_irqflag() applies
the wrong DAIF mask and leaves interrupts permanently disabled.

Extend struct prev_kprobe with a saved_irqflag field and save/restore it
alongside kp and status. This ensures the outer kprobe's original
interrupt state is preserved across reentry.

This mirrors the x86 fix in commit 6a5022a56ac3
("kprobes/x86: Allow to handle reentered kprobe on single-stepping").

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

wifi: libertas: reject short monitor TX frames

In monitor mode, lbs_hard_start_xmit() casts skb->data to a
radiotap TX header, skips that header, and then copies the 802.11
destination address from offset 4 in the remaining frame.  The
generic length check only rejects zero-length and oversized skbs, so
a short monitor frame can be read past the end of the skb data.

Require enough bytes for the radiotap TX header and the destination
address field before using the monitor-mode header layout.

BASE_ERROR_EVENT carries a variable number of message reports,
with the count encoded in error_status. The notification parser used

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

firmware: arm_scmi: Validate SENSOR_UPDATE payload size

SENSOR_UPDATE carries one or more sensor readings after the fixed
notification header. The parser derives the expected reading count
from the sensor description, but it did not verify that the received

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

drm/amd/ras: reset CPER ring on corrupt entry size

When CPER ring overflow handling advances the read pointer, it trusts the
parsed entry size from the current ring contents. Corrupt CPER data can
produce an entry size that does not advance rptr after dword conversion
and pointer masking.

In that case the recovery loop keeps testing the same location while
holding the CPER ring mutex. This can hang the worker that is writing the
next CPER record.

Detect a no-progress rptr update and reset the CPER ring to an empty
state instead. This drops the corrupt contents and lets the writer leave
the recovery path without spinning.

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

thunderbolt: Keep the domain reference while processing hotplug

We process hotplug events in a workqueue that may run after the domain
has been removed by tb_domain_remove(). For example if user unloads the
driver while at the same time plugging  a device router we may have
scheduled tb_handle_hotplug() to run. Avoid possible UAF in this case by
taking the domain reference before scheduling the hotplug handler in
tb_queue_hotplug().

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

ksmbd: don't hold ci->m_lock while waiting for a lease break ack

When a cifs.ko client caches a read-handle (RH) lease via deferred close
and a conflicting open arrives, ksmbd breaks the lease and waits for the
acknowledgment in wait_for_break_ack() for up to OPLOCK_WAIT_TIME (35s).
__smb_break_all_levII_oplock() runs that wait while holding ci->m_lock
for read.

cifs.ko reacts to a handle-lease break by closing the deferred handle
rather than sending a lease break acknowledgment. That close path
(close_id_del_oplock() -> opinfo_del()) takes ci->m_lock for write and
is exactly what would wake the waiter, but it blocks on the read lock
held by the waiting thread. The break is then resolved only by the 35s
timeout, so xfstests generic/001 takes ~78s with leases enabled versus
~4s with oplocks only.

Collect the target opinfos (each pinned with a reference) while holding
ci->m_lock, then break them after releasing it, matching how
smb_grant_oplock() already breaks a conflicting lease using only a
reference.  The reference keeps the opinfo (and its conn and lease)
alive across the unlocked window, and a close racing the break is
handled by the existing OPLOCK_CLOSING state check. Apply the same fix
to the parent lease break paths.

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

xen/gntalloc: validate grant count before allocation

gntalloc_ioctl_alloc() allocates the grant-id array before checking
whether the requested count fits within the global grant limit. Counts
above that limit cannot succeed, so reject them before the
user-controlled allocation reaches kcalloc().

requested count cannot wrap. Also cast the count before advancing the

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

ksmbd: fix lease break and ack state handling

Do not skip valid lease states containing WRITE_CACHING when breaking
level-II/read leases for writes and truncates.

Handle lease break acknowledgments according to the SMB2 rule that the
acknowledged state must be a subset of the server's break target. Apply

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

mailbox: imx: Add a channel shutdown field

sashiko complained about possible teardown problem. The scenario

 CPU 0                              CPU 1
  imx_mu_isr()                   imx_mu_shutdown()
                                   imx_mu_xcr_rmw(priv, IMX_MU_RCR, 0, IMX_MU_xCR_RIEn(priv->dcfg->type, cp->idx));
    imx_mu_specific_rx()
      imx_mu_xcr_rmw(priv, IMX_MU_RCR, IMX_MU_xCR_RIEn(priv->dcfg->type, 0), 0);
                                   free_irq()

The RX event remains enabled because in this short window the RX event
was disabled in ->shutdown() while the interrupt was active and then
enabled again by the ISR while ->shutdown waited in free_irq().

This race requires timing and if happens can be problematic on shared
handlers if the "removed" channel triggers an interrupt. In this case
the irq-core will shutdown the interrupt with the "nobody cared"
message.

Introduce imx_mu_con_priv::shutdown to signal that the channel is
shutting down. This flag is set with the lock held (by
imx_mu_xcr_clr_shut()). The unmask side uses imx_mu_xcr_set_act() which
only enables the event if the channel has not been shutdown and
serialises on the same lock.

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

mailbox: imx: Use devm_pm_runtime_enable()

sashiko complained about early usage of the device while probe isn't
completed. This can be mitigated by delaying the pm_runtime_enable()
into the removal path instead doing it early. This ensures that in an
error case the device is removed (and imx_mu_shutdown()) before
pm_runtime_disable() so we don't have to do this manually.

For the order to work, lets move devm_mbox_controller_register() until
after the pm-runtime part. So the reverse order will be mbox-controller
removal followed by disabling pm runtime.

Use devm_pm_runtime_enable(), remove manual pm_runtime_disable()
invocations and move the pm_runtime handling in probe before
devm_mbox_controller_register().

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

drm/amdkfd: Properly acquire queue buffers in CRIU restore

When kfd_queue_acquire_buffers() was split off from
set_queue_properties_from_user(), set_queue_properties_from_criu()
was missed. Thus, set_queue_properties_from_criu() is not
filling out the buffer fields of queue_properties, which
can come up when subsequent code expects them to be non-null.

Add the proper call to kfd_queue_acquire_buffers(), and also
use the right cast types in set_queue_properties_from_criu()
(which were missed at the same time)

(cherry picked from commit 88ed96abbbe27b70193544fbc1ee06448c274714)

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

net: lan966x: restore RX state on reload failure

lan966x_fdma_reload() backs up rx->page_pool and rx->fdma before
reallocating the RX resources for the new MTU. If the allocation fails,
the restore path puts these fields back before restarting RX.

However, the reload path also updates rx->page_order and rx->max_mtu
before calling lan966x_fdma_rx_alloc(). These fields are not restored on
failure, so RX can be restarted with the old pages, old FDMA state and
old page pool, but with the page geometry from the failed new MTU.

This can make the XDP path advertise a frame size derived from the new
page_order while the actual RX pages still come from the old allocation.
For example, after a failed reload to a jumbo MTU, xdp_init_buff() may be
called with a frame size larger than the restored RX pages.

lan966x_fdma_rx_alloc_page_pool() also registers the newly allocated page
pool with each port's XDP RXQ before fdma_alloc_coherent() is called. If
fdma_alloc_coherent() fails, the new page pool is destroyed, but the
rollback path does not restore the per-port XDP RXQ mem model
registration either.

Save and restore rx->page_order and rx->max_mtu, and restore the old page
pool registration for each port's XDP RXQ before RX is started again.
This keeps the restored RX state consistent after a failed reload.

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

btrfs: protect sb_write_pointer() with invalidate lock

sb_write_pointer() reads the super block from the block device page cache
using read_cache_page_gfp(). This has the same race with BLKBSZSET as the
one fixed by commit 3f29d661e568 ("btrfs: sync read disk super and set
block size").

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

net: microchip: sparx5: clean up PSFP resources on flower setup failure

sparx5_tc_flower_psfp_setup() allocates PSFP stream gate, flow meter and
stream filter resources before adding VCAP actions. If a later step
fails, the resources allocated earlier in the function are not unwound.

Add error paths to release the stream filter, flow meter and stream gate
when setup fails after they have been acquired.

Also make sparx5_psfp_fm_add() return the acquired flow-meter id before
the existing-flow-meter early return. When an existing flow meter is
reused, sparx5_psfp_fm_get() increments its pool reference count, but the
caller previously kept psfp_fmid as 0. If a later setup step failed, the
error path could try to delete flow-meter id 0 instead of the reused flow
meter, leaving the incremented reference behind.

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

net: cpsw_new: unregister devlink on port registration failure

cpsw_probe() registers devlink before registering the CPSW ports.

If cpsw_register_ports() fails, the error path only unregisters the
notifiers and then releases the lower level resources. It does not undo
the successful cpsw_register_devlink() call, leaving the devlink instance
and its parameters registered after probe has failed.

Add a devlink cleanup label for the path where devlink registration has
already succeeded, and use it when port registration fails.

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

drm/amdkfd: Unwind debug trap enable on copy_to_user failure

If kfd_dbg_trap_enable() fails while copying runtime_info to userspace,
it had already activated the trap, set debug_trap_enabled, taken an extra
process reference, and opened the debug event file. Return -EFAULT without
unwinding that state, leaving inconsistent trap state and a refcount
imbalance that could break later DISABLE/ENABLE.

On copy_to_user failure, deactivate the trap and undo the rest of the
enable setup before returning.

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

ALSA: seq: oss: Reject reads that cannot fit the next event

snd_seq_oss_read() checks whether the next queued OSS sequencer event
fits in the remaining userspace buffer before removing it from the read
queue.

The check is inverted. It currently stops when the event is smaller than
the remaining buffer, so a normal 4-byte event is not copied for an
8-byte read buffer. Conversely, an 8-byte event can be copied for a
smaller read count.

Break only when the remaining userspace buffer is smaller than the next
event, and report -EINVAL if no complete event has been copied. This
prevents an undersized read from looking like end-of-file while leaving
the event queued for a later read with a large enough buffer.

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

mm/damon/ops-common: use a page-aligned address in damon_ptep_mkold()

__damon_va_prepare_access_check() picks a random byte address within the
region and stores it in r->sampling_addr.  damon_va_mkold() passes it into
a page table walk, which hands it to damon_ptep_mkold() as the address of
the page to sample:

  damon_va_mkold(mm, r->sampling_addr)
    damon_va_walk_page_range(mm, addr, addr + 1)
      damon_mkold_pmd_entry()
        damon_ptep_mkold(pte, vma, addr)
          ptep_test_and_clear_young(vma, addr, pte)
          mmu_notifier_clear_young(mm, addr, addr + PAGE_SIZE)

For arm64, before commit 6f0e1142173a ("arm64: mm: support batch clearing
of the young flag for large folios"), the contpte helper walked exactly
CONT_PTES entries from the aligned-down page table pointer and used @addr
only to pass down to each entry, so an unaligned value was harmless:

        ptep = contpte_align_down(ptep);
        addr = ALIGN_DOWN(addr, CONT_PTE_SIZE);
        for (i = 0; i < CONT_PTES; i++, ptep++, addr += PAGE_SIZE)

Now the range to walk is derived from @addr instead: end = addr + nr *
PAGE_SIZE, rounded up to CONT_PTE_SIZE.  For a sample in the last page of
a contpte block, the sub-page offset puts end just past the block
boundary, so the round-up lands a whole block further and the walk clears
PTE_AF in CONT_PTES entries beyond the sampled block.  For the last block
in a page table page, those entries are past the end of that page, so the
walk writes into the page that follows.

Triggered by the full 7.1/7.2 kernel selftest suite on arm64 (EC2
c/m6g.4xlarge).  The kernel sometimes crashes at or shortly after the
DAMON test.

What the overrun does depends on the page that happens to follow the page
table, so there is no single signature.  If that page is read-only, the
write faults in the sampling path itself:

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

drm/xe: harden adjust_idledly() against divide-by-zero and overflow

adjust_idledly() has several corner-case issues flagged during review:

  1. If xe_gt_clock_init() failed to recognise the crystal clock,
     gt->info.timestamp_base is 0, which makes idledly_units_ps also 0.
     The subsequent DIV_ROUND_CLOSEST(..., idledly_units_ps) is then a
     divide-by-zero and panics the kernel.

  2. The tick-to-ns conversions are done in u32:
        idledly * idledly_units_ps, (maxcnt - 1) * 1000
     Both overflow u32 before DIV_ROUND_CLOSEST() sees them.

  3. If IDLE_WAIT_TIME reads back as 0, maxcnt evaluates to 0 and
     the maxcnt - 1 clamp wraps to 0xFFFFFFFF in u32.

  4. The register only stores whole ticks, so the clamped ns value has
     to be converted to ticks and back. DIV_ROUND_CLOSEST() can round
     that conversion up past maxcnt:

       maxcnt = 640 ns, one tick = 666664 ps

       clamp:        maxcnt - 1        = 639 ns
       ns -> ticks:  639000 / 666664   = 0.958 -> rounds to 1 tick
       tick -> ns:    1 * 666664 / 1000 = 667 ns

     667 ns is programmed into RING_IDLEDLY, but 667 >= maxcnt (640),
     so xe_gt_WARN_ON() fires again on every subsequent init.

Return early if timestamp_base is 0 (the unknown-crystal path).
Do the conversions in u64 via the *_ULL() helpers so they cannot wrap.
Clamp with a floor (DIV_ROUND_DOWN_ULL) so the programmed delay stays
strictly below maxcnt, and guard the maxcnt == 0 case with a zero delay
while still writing RING_IDLEDLY so INHIBIT_SWITCH_UNTIL_PREEMPTED is
cleared.

v2: Drop the redundant warn on the timestamp_base == 0 path;
    xe_gt_clock_init() already warns on an unrecognised crystal clock.
    Keep the early return to avoid the divide-by-zero. - Vinay

v3: Field-mask the RING_IDLEDLY write with REG_FIELD_PREP(IDLE_DELAY, ...)
    instead of writing the raw tick count, which could clobber
    INHIBIT_SWITCH_UNTIL_PREEMPTED and reserved bits. Split the
    inhibit-switch clear from the maxcnt clamp so a set inhibit bit no
    longer forces a needless delay overwrite when the delay itself is
    already valid. Use gt_to_xe(gt) instead of gt_to_xe(hwe->gt).

(cherry picked from commit d864065ea25e9d12897c175de9176ce46677e176)

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

netfs: Fix missing alloc tagging of direct mempool allocations

Commit 1d78d56c43ef ("netfs: Fix folio_queue ENOMEM in writeback by
adding a mempool") added a mempool for the folio_queues and made the
request, subrequest and folio_queue allocations distinguish between
writeback and everything else.  Writeback is part of memory reclaim
and must not fail due to ENOMEM, so it allocates under GFP_NOFS
through mempool_alloc(), which may dip into the pool's reserve and,
if that runs empty, wait for elements to be returned.  The
GFP_KERNEL paths, which can return -ENOMEM to their callers, invoke
the pool's ->alloc() callback directly instead.

The direct call, however, skips the alloc_hooks() wrapper that the
mempool_alloc() macro provides.  The pool callbacks, mempool_alloc_slab()
and mempool_kmalloc(), call kmem_cache_alloc_noprof() and kmalloc_noprof()
and rely on current->alloc_tag having been set by the caller.  With
CONFIG_MEM_ALLOC_PROFILING_DEBUG=y this leads to

    current->alloc_tag not set
    WARNING: ./include/linux/alloc_tag.h:161 at __alloc_tagging_slab_alloc_hook
    alloc_tag was not set
    WARNING: ./include/linux/alloc_tag.h:166 at __alloc_tagging_slab_free_hook

at allocation and free time respectively, as reported when reading
files on a CIFS mount.  The allocations are also missing from
/proc/allocinfo.

Wrap the direct ->alloc() invocations in alloc_hooks() with a new
mempool_alloc_noreserve() helper in include/linux/mempool.h, next to
the other alloc_hooks()-wrapped macros such as mempool_alloc().  The
GFP_KERNEL paths keep their failable allocation semantics, they just
get tagged now.

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

ovl: fix UAF in ovl_do_mkdir() debug print

ovl_do_mkdir() prints the input dentry with %pd after vfs_mkdir().
Since commit fe497f0759e0 ("VFS: change vfs_mkdir() to unlock on
failure."), vfs_mkdir() calls end_creating() on the input dentry on
failure and may replace it on success, so the post-call %pd can
use-after-free the dentry when CONFIG_OVERLAY_FS_DEBUG is enabled.

Print the dentry before the call and only the result afterward.
